misconceptions.wrong_belief: an assignment cannot be used inside a larger expression
misconceptions.correct_rule: An assignment is an expression whose value is the value assigned, so (x = v) both stores v in x and gives v.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a = b copies the value of a into b.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Assignment stores the value of the right side into the variable on the left.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: When the then branch runs, the code after the if is skipped.
misconceptions.correct_rule: After the if finishes, execution continues with the next statement either way.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes a + b = c; or 7 = a; as if = were a math equation.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The left side of an assignment must be a single variable; only the right side can be an expression.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: When an if condition is false (and there is no else), control jumps back to the start of the program.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A false condition skips the then branch and execution continues with the statement after the if statement.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Java is case-sensitive: names of variables, methods and classes that differ only in capitalization are different names.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An if statement watches its condition while the program runs and fires as soon as the condition becomes true (if = whenever).
misconceptions.correct_rule: An if condition is tested once, when control reaches the if statement; later changes to the variables do not trigger the branch.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An IF statement earlier in the program stays active and fires later, e.g. inside a later loop, when its condition becomes true.
misconceptions.correct_rule: An if is evaluated once when control reaches it; afterwards it is inactive unless control returns to it.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Indents nested blocks inconsistently, so the visual nesting differs from the real nesting.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a large integer literal is automatically long

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Testing one case is enough; Java will repeat the test for the other values by itself.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a single literal or variable "isn't an expression"

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Java has no long literals

misconceptions.wrong_belief: keywords may be reused as identifiers

misconceptions.wrong_belief: nested calls run outside-in, not arguments-first

wrong rule: = compares two values instead of assigning. Right rule: x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them.
wrong rule: an assignment cannot be used inside a larger expression. Right rule: An assignment is an expression whose value is the value assigned, so (x = v) both stores v in x and gives v.
wrong rule: a = b copies the value of a into b. Right rule: Assignment stores the value of the right side into the variable on the left.
wrong rule: a = b adds the value of b to the value already in a (the accumulator model). Right rule: a = b replaces the old value of a with the value of b; the old value is lost.

wrong rule: An assignment states a lasting equality between its two sides, so y = x - y can be solved like the equation x = 2y and x = x + 5 relates two equal quantities. Right rule: An assignment is a one-time action: evaluate the right side with current values, then store the result in the left variable.
wrong rule: b = a exchanges the values of a and b. Right rule: b = a copies a into b and leaves a unchanged; an exchange needs a temporary variable and three assignments.
wrong rule: After b = a, a no longer holds a value, as if the value had been moved. Right rule: Assignment copies; the variable on the right keeps its value.

wrong rule: a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = a[i]; exchanges the two values. Right rule: A temporary variable must save a[i] before it is overwritten.
wrong rule: assigning a reference copies the object. Right rule: b = a; copies only the reference, so a and b refer to the same array and b[i] = v also changes a[i].
wrong rule: A variable keeps its first value after a new assignment (the static model). Right rule: Each assignment or read replaces the variable's current value.

Swapping the two sides (a = b versus b = a) changes which variable changes. Reordering assignments changes the final values. An assignment cannot be undone, because the old value is lost unless it was first saved in a temporary.
wrong rule: a single literal or variable "isn't an expression". Right rule: A single variable or literal is an expression whose value is just that value.

(here mixing in: "a single literal or variable "isn't an expression"")

wrong rule: () are optional on a no-argument call like println. Right rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.

wrong rule: The type of a numerical expression depends on the type expected by the surrounding context, so double d = a / b; keeps the fraction. Right rule: The type of a numerical expression is determined by the expression, so double d = a / b; with int a and b still divides as ints.
wrong rule: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value. Right rule: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.
wrong rule: nested calls run outside-in, not arguments-first. Right rule: In f(g(x)), g(x) is evaluated first and its result is passed to f.

wrong rule: An assignment states a lasting equality between its two sides, so y = x - y can be solved like the equation x = 2y and x = x + 5 relates two equal quantities. Right rule: An assignment is a one-time action: evaluate the right side with current values, then store the result in the left variable.

Adding parentheses that match the default grouping keeps the value, and rewriting with an equivalent formula (4 * (x - 3) as 4*x - 12) keeps it for ints. Changing one operand's type (3 to 3.0) can change both the result's type and its value.
wrong rule: The computer fills in omitted steps or values the programmer meant. Right rule: The computer executes only the statements written; every needed step and value must be written.

wrong rule: Statements in a program can run in any order, so their order makes no difference. Right rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom, in the order written.

wrong rule: Line breaks and indentation change what the program does, so each statement must be on its own line. Right rule: Java compilers treat all whitespace outside quotes as equivalent; statements are separated by ;, not by line breaks.

wrong rule: The program knows what later lines will do and acts on that goal at the current line. Right rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.
Swapping two statements that touch the same variable or the output generally changes the result; swapping independent statements, or changing only whitespace between them, keeps it.

wrong rule: a large integer literal is automatically long. Right rule: A sequence of digits is an int literal only if its value falls within the int range; for larger values the book advises the long type.
wrong rule: Java has no float literals. Right rule: A decimal literal ending in f is a float; without the f it is a double.
wrong rule: Java has no long literals. Right rule: An integer literal ending in L is a long.
wrong rule: 207. and 2.3e4 are int values because they are whole numbers. Right rule: A decimal point or scientific notation makes the literal a double.

Rewriting a literal in another form keeps the value but changes the type, and so the operation: 10 / 3 is 3 but 10.0 / 3 is 3.333..., and "5" + 1 is "51" but 5 + 1 is 6.

wrong rule: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method. Right rule: Java is case-sensitive: names of variables, methods and classes that differ only in capitalization are different names.
wrong rule: keywords may be reused as identifiers. Right rule: Keywords are reserved by Java and cannot be used as variable names.

Points to LT (a name refers to the declaration with exactly that spelling in scope). Applied unevenly, a student treats Count and count as one variable in one statement but as two in another. (here mixing in: "System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method")

Renaming an identifier consistently at its declaration and every use leaves behavior unchanged. Renaming only some occurrences, or changing only the capitalization, breaks compilation with 'cannot find symbol'.
wrong rule: A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global. Right rule: A local variable's scope runs from its declaration to the end of the enclosing block.

(here mixing in: "A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global")

wrong rule: A statement placed after the if statement belongs to its branch, so it runs only when the condition is true. Right rule: The branch ends at its closing brace (or after its single statement); the next statement runs whatever the condition was.

wrong rule: Some statements inside the loop braces are not repeated; they run once, before or after the loop. Right rule: Every statement inside the loop braces is part of the body and runs on every pass.

wrong rule: A statement written after the loop is repeated with the loop body. Right rule: The body ends at the closing brace (or after its single statement); code after it runs once, after the loop ends.

Adding braces around a single-statement body keeps behaviour; adding a second statement to a braceless body changes it (the new statement runs outside); moving a declaration into a block makes later uses outside the block fail to compile.
wrong rule: Statements in a program can run in any order. Right rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom.

wrong rule: The program knows or sees what later lines will do and acts on those goals at the current line, e.g. it stops 'at ten' because it wants to draw a box. Right rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.

Applies the sequencing rule (LT) unevenly: e.g. runs a later line before an earlier one, lets an if that was already passed fire again later, or ends the program when a loop or a false if ends instead of continuing with the next statement. (here mixing in: "Statements in a program can run in any order")
wrong rule: When the then branch runs, the code after the if is skipped. Right rule: After the if finishes, execution continues with the next statement either way.
wrong rule: logical AND/OR always evaluate both sides (Java short-circuits them). Right rule: In p && q, q is evaluated only when p is true; in p || q, q is evaluated only when p is false.

wrong rule: Testing one case is enough; Java will repeat the test for the other values by itself. Right rule: A statement runs once each time control reaches it; repeating a test for many values needs a loop.

wrong rule: An IF statement earlier in the program stays active and fires later, e.g. inside a later loop, when its condition becomes true. Right rule: An if is evaluated once when control reaches it; afterwards it is inactive unless control returns to it.

wrong rule: When an if condition is false (and there is no else), control jumps back to the start of the program. Right rule: A false condition skips the then branch and execution continues with the statement after the if statement.

wrong rule: An if statement watches its condition while the program runs and fires as soon as the condition becomes true (if = whenever). Right rule: An if condition is tested once, when control reaches the if statement; later changes to the variables do not trigger the branch.
wrong rule: When a loop finishes the program ends, so code after the loop never runs. Right rule: When the loop condition becomes false, control continues with the first statement after the loop.

wrong rule: A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats. Right rule: Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once.

Reordering two statements generally changes the result whenever one reads a variable that the other writes (e.g. swapping x = x + 1 and print(x)); reordering is safe only for statements that touch disjoint variables. Moving a statement into or out of a branch or loop body changes how many times it runs (0, 1 or n).

wrong rule: After the matching case runs, the switch ends even without break. Right rule: Without break, all the statements after the matching label run, including those under later case labels, until a break or the end of the switch.

Applies the LT rule unevenly: on a trace the selector is matched correctly but execution stops at the next case label on some runs and falls through on others, or default is run even though a case matched. (here mixing in: "After the matching case runs, the switch ends even without break")

When every case ends with break, reordering the cases does not change behaviour (labels are distinct constants). Removing one break changes behaviour for that value only. Adding a default changes only values with no matching label.
